title: The Disordered Universe 2025: An Intro and a Vision
abstract: The Disordered Universe is a novel research direction that exploits ideas and techniques coming from apparently unrelated research areas, ranging from cosmology to scattering amplitudes in particle physics and disordered complex systems, with the aim of addressing open questions in cosmology at all scales, from the very infra-red (or very late time) to the early universe. This paper acts as a general introduction and vision for a set of lectures delivered at the first La Ricotta Summer School "The Disordered Universe 2025", held from 21 July to 10 August 2025. These lectures involved open quantum systems, analytic properties of scattering amplitudes and correlation functions, foundations and quantum aspects of the de Sitter universe, as well as statistical physics out of equilibrium and spin glasses. While the lecture notes related to each course taught at the school will be published separately and are inevitably devoted to both conceptual and technical aspects of each of these topics, the school was not meant to be a collage of independent topics: the present paper has the purpose of outlining the global vision, how cosmology ends up being a unifier and benefits from both their viewpoint and techniques, how all the concepts and techniques originally coming from these four different areas are part of the same cosmological narrative, why this point of view deserves to be explored, and drawing perspectives for the future. We consider it crucial to build a microscopic theory for the early universe and maybe one that embraces all scales.
summary: This paper proposes the 'Disordered Universe' as a unifying research program for cosmology, integrating techniques from particle physics, open quantum systems, and disordered statistical mechanics. It aims to build a comprehensive microscopic theory for the early universe by analyzing global observables and correlation functions across all cosmic epochs. The work suggests that insights from spin-glass theory can provide the necessary mathematical structure to overcome current limitations in describing quantum gravity effects.
main_problem: To develop a unifying framework to address open questions in cosmology across all scales, from the very late time to the early universe.
main_result: The paper argues that cosmology benefits from techniques developed in seemingly unrelated fields like particle scattering amplitudes and spin-glass theory to build a comprehensive microscopic theory for the early universe.
method: It employs analogies between the analytic properties of scattering amplitudes in particle physics and the correlation functions observed in cosmological observables, particularly in the context of disordered systems.
model_or_system: The primary system is the Universe, focusing on the physics of the early universe (e.g., inflation, de Sitter space). The theoretical framework integrates concepts from quantum field theory in curved spacetime, open quantum systems, and disordered statistical mechanics.
key_observables: Primordial fluctuations ($\langle\Phi\Phi \cdots \Phiangle$), CMB temperature/density fluctuations ($\langle\delta T\delta T \cdots \delta Tangle$), and large-scale structure observables.
important_parameters: Tensor-to-scalar ratio ($r$), scalar amplitude ($A_s$), and the cosmological constant ($\Lambda$).
main_assumptions: The standard approach to inflationary correlators is insufficient, necessitating the incorporation of principles from out-of-equilibrium complex systems and particle physics methods.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the connection between correlation functions from inflation, CMB, and large-scale structure. Figure 2 diagrams the interplay between cosmology, scattering amplitudes, and open quantum systems.
paper_structure: The paper serves as a general introduction and vision, outlining how cosmology acts as a unifier by drawing techniques from four distinct areas: cosmology, scattering amplitudes, open quantum systems, and statistical physics.
why_interesting: The explicit drawing of parallels between the complex, non-equilibrium dynamics of the early universe and the mathematical structures found in spin glasses and disordered systems provides novel theoretical tools for analyzing quantum field theory in curved spacetime.
